dossier:
I located and read the GDPval paper, “GDPval: Evaluating AI Model Performance on Real-World Economically Valuable Tasks” (arXiv:2510.04374v1), focusing on section 3.4 and Appendix A.3, with nearby setup details where relevant. The source does **not** provide a single full agent trajectory, task ID, transcript, or exact sequence of tool invocations. It reports aggregate behavior of GPT-5 runs on GDPval and describes a prompt/scaffolding intervention designed in response to observed failures. The account below is therefore limited to what the paper states.

## Chronological account

### 1. The agent was evaluated on GDPval tasks

GPT-5, including a high-reasoning-effort setting, was evaluated on GDPval: a benchmark of real-world, economically valuable knowledge-work tasks. The tasks came with prompts and, often, reference files. The model was expected to produce professional deliverables, frequently in file formats such as PDF, PowerPoint, Word, Excel, or similar work products.

For OpenAI models, the evaluation harness enabled:

- the web search tool,
- the code interpreter tool,
- background sampling,
- additional preinstalled libraries beyond the base image.

The paper also notes that for plotted results, models were sampled three times per prompt, and each sample was graded by three different human graders.

### 2. GPT-5 high produced deliverables for the tasks

In the baseline GDPval runs, GPT-5 high attempted to complete the assigned tasks and generate the requested deliverables. The paper describes GPT-5 high as doing comparatively well on accuracy and instruction following: in the model-strengths analysis, GPT-5 and Grok had the fewest accuracy errors, and GPT-5 high had fewer instruction-following issues than several other models.

However, GPT-5 high’s losing outputs were often rejected for issues in the produced deliverables rather than because it had failed to follow the core task instructions.

### 3. Human experts compared GPT-5 outputs against human deliverables

GDPval outputs were evaluated through blind pairwise comparisons by professional industry experts. These graders compared model-generated deliverables against human expert deliverables and indicated which was better. Expert justifications were then used in a clustering analysis of why models won or lost.

The paper reports that, across models, experts often preferred the human deliverable because models failed to fully follow instructions. For GPT-5 high specifically, the observed loss pattern was different: GPT-5 high “lost mainly from formatting errors” and had the fewest instruction-following issues among the compared models.

### 4. The observed GPT-5 failure points were concentrated in formatting and visual quality

Section 3.4 says that many observed GPT-5 failure modes were “obvious formatting errors.” The paper gives two concrete aggregate examples:

- Black-square artifacts affected more than half of GPT-5-generated PDFs before prompt tuning.
- Egregious formatting errors affected 86% of PowerPoint files before prompt tuning.

The paper also states that all models sometimes hallucinated data or miscalculated, though GPT-5 and Grok showed the fewest accuracy errors among the compared systems.

### 5. The model often did not use multimodal checking on its own

A key behavioral signal reported in section 3.4 is that, before the prompt/scaffolding change, only 15% of agents used their multimodal capabilities to inspect their own deliverables.

The paper does not provide individual examples of tool calls, but this statistic indicates that in many runs the agent submitted visual deliverables without first rendering or visually checking them in the way later prompted. The source presents this as part of the observed context around formatting failures.

### 6. The researchers introduced a prompt-tuning intervention

In response to these observed failures, the authors created a general prompt intended to elicit better capabilities from GPT-5. Appendix A.3 gives the prompt. It was not specific to any one GDPval task; it was a general instruction set for multimodal economic tasks.

The prompt instructed the agent to avoid formatting and rendering pitfalls, including:

- never use the nonstandard hyphen character U+2011;
- avoid emojis, nonstandard bullets, and special characters unless strongly justified;
- make diagrams and plots large enough to be legible;
- avoid overly complicated visuals made by overlaying many shapes;
- always use LibreOffice to create PDFs;
- use cross-platform fonts, recommending Noto Sans or Noto Serif;
- ensure requested deliverables are files in the container, not only text in the response;
- keep deliverable text concise;
- produce a complete, self-contained submission even if some part is limited by the environment;
- use standard file types if none are specified;
- for video files, extract image frames and inspect them for visual corruption.

### 7. The intervention also required explicit formatting checks before submission

Appendix A.3’s prompt made several pre-submission checks mandatory.

The agent was instructed to:

1. Convert all visual deliverables — including PPTX, DOCX, PDF, XLSX, and similar files — to PNGs using LibreOffice, with each page or slide as a separate PNG.
2. Display the PNGs and inspect them for cut-off text, overlapping text, distorted graphics, blank pages, hard-to-read contrast, or other formatting problems.
3. Run programmatic checks for highly visual submissions, including checks for blank pages, cut-off page elements, overlapping text or graphics, and compliance with page or slide limits.
4. Summarize the prompt’s deliverable instructions and match them to the corresponding part of the deliverable.
5. Immediately before submission, check that the deliverables are exactly the intended files, with no extras, and open each file to verify it is not corrupted and is well formatted.

If any issue was found, the prompt instructed the agent to fix it and repeat the checks.

Finally, the prompt required the last line of output text to include `CONFIDENCE[XX]`, where `XX` was an integer from 0 to 100 indicating confidence that the submission was correct, followed instructions, and was well formatted.

### 8. The researchers also changed the scaffolding

Section 3.4 says the authors improved scaffolding in two additional ways:

- They enabled GET requests in the container.
- They performed best-of-N sampling with `N=4`, using a GPT-5 judge.

Appendix A.3 describes the best-of-N process: a GPT-5 grader was prompted with the task prompt, reference files, and deliverable files for four different submissions, then asked to pick the best one.

### 9. The post-intervention outcomes improved, but did not remove all problems

After the prompt-tuning and scaffolding changes, the paper reports several measurable changes:

- Black-square artifacts in GPT-5 PDF responses were fully eliminated.
- Egregious formatting errors in PowerPoint files decreased from 86% to 64%.
- Use of multimodal capabilities to inspect deliverables increased from 15% to 97%.
- Human preference win rates improved by 5 percentage points in the prompt-tuning experiment shown in Figure 9b.

The final outcome reported in the source is therefore not a single failed run being fixed, but an aggregate pattern: GPT-5 high was already relatively strong on accuracy and instruction following, but many of its losing GDPval outputs had visible formatting or file-quality problems. A general prompt plus scaffolding changes caused more frequent deliverable inspection and improved several measured formatting and preference outcomes, while some PowerPoint formatting errors remained.

I located and read the GDPval paper, “GDPval: Evaluating AI Model Performance on Real-World Economically Valuable Tasks” (arXiv:2510.04374v1), focusing on section 3.4 and Appendix A.3, with nearby setup details where relevant. The source does **not** provide a single full agent trajectory, task ID, transcript, or exact sequence of tool invocations. It reports aggregate behavior of GPT-5 runs on GDPval and describes a prompt/scaffolding intervention designed in response to observed failures. The account below is therefore limited to what the paper states.

## Chronological account

### 1. The agent was evaluated on GDPval tasks

GPT-5, including a high-reasoning-effort setting, was evaluated on GDPval: a benchmark of real-world, economically valuable knowledge-work tasks. The tasks came with prompts and, often, reference files. The model was expected to produce professional deliverables, frequently in file formats such as PDF, PowerPoint, Word, Excel, or similar work products.

For OpenAI models, the evaluation harness enabled:

- the web search tool,
- the code interpreter tool,
- background sampling,
- additional preinstalled libraries beyond the base image.

The paper also notes that for plotted results, models were sampled three times per prompt, and each sample was graded by three different human graders.

### 2. GPT-5 high produced deliverables for the tasks

In the baseline GDPval runs, GPT-5 high attempted to complete the assigned tasks and generate the requested deliverables. The paper describes GPT-5 high as doing comparatively well on accuracy and instruction following: in the model-strengths analysis, GPT-5 and Grok had the fewest accuracy errors, and GPT-5 high had fewer instruction-following issues than several other models.

However, GPT-5 high’s losing outputs were often rejected for issues in the produced deliverables rather than because it had failed to follow the core task instructions.

### 3. Human experts compared GPT-5 outputs against human deliverables

GDPval outputs were evaluated through blind pairwise comparisons by professional industry experts. These graders compared model-generated deliverables against human expert deliverables and indicated which was better. Expert justifications were then used in a clustering analysis of why models won or lost.

The paper reports that, across models, experts often preferred the human deliverable because models failed to fully follow instructions. For GPT-5 high specifically, the observed loss pattern was different: GPT-5 high “lost mainly from formatting errors” and had the fewest instruction-following issues among the compared models.

### 4. The observed GPT-5 failure points were concentrated in formatting and visual quality

Section 3.4 says that many observed GPT-5 failure modes were “obvious formatting errors.” The paper gives two concrete aggregate examples:

- Black-square artifacts affected more than half of GPT-5-generated PDFs before prompt tuning.
- Egregious formatting errors affected 86% of PowerPoint files before prompt tuning.

The paper also states that all models sometimes hallucinated data or miscalculated, though GPT-5 and Grok showed the fewest accuracy errors among the compared systems.

### 5. The model often did not use multimodal checking on its own

A key behavioral signal reported in section 3.4 is that, before the prompt/scaffolding change, only 15% of agents used their multimodal capabilities to inspect their own deliverables.

The paper does not provide individual examples of tool calls, but this statistic indicates that in many runs the agent submitted visual deliverables without first rendering or visually checking them in the way later prompted. The source presents this as part of the observed context around formatting failures.

### 6. The researchers introduced a prompt-tuning intervention

In response to these observed failures, the authors created a general prompt intended to elicit better capabilities from GPT-5. Appendix A.3
